report:
Conclusion: the “no” answer is not supported. Across randomized trials and systematic reviews, adding HIV self-testing (HIVST) as an option generally increases HIV-testing uptake versus standard services alone—especially among key populations and people not reached by clinics—though effects vary by delivery model, cost, reminders, and linkage support.

The strongest synthesis found HIVST increased testing uptake overall (RR 2.09; 95% CI 1.69–2.58; 13 RCTs; moderate-certainty evidence) in the general population (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext). A key-populations review likewise found RCT evidence of increased uptake, testing frequency, and positivity, without clear increases in social harm (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z). WHO’s policy update recommends HIVST as safe, accurate, and effective for reaching people who may not otherwise test (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-CDS-HIV-19.36). A later narrative review summarizes that numerous RCTs found offering HIVST raises testing rates, while emphasizing confirmatory testing and linkage to care (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8915955/).

So: yes—an additional offer of HIV self-testing usually causes more people to take an HIV test, but it is not a universal guarantee and works best when kits are free/easy to get and follow-up pathways are strong.
